preamble: Six-letter solution spaces in the grid have undefined clues to forenames and surnames of eight men of a kind. Only one of these names in each case is to be entered in the diagram.

clue.text: Rugby forward to be holding castle (6,6)

parts.note: the forename, not entered: RU (Rugby Union) plus PERT (forward, cheeky) gives RUPERT

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: taken as written
the rook is the castle in chess

explanation.surface: A rugby forward is about to clutch a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke, the First World War poet, went to Rugby School. The first two words build his forename, the rest his surname, which is the name entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says each six-letter clue names a man of a kind; the eight are all English-language poets, and Brooke wrote The Soldier.

clue.text: Pastoral, but reduced by severe pain

indicators.note: something reduced is made shorter, so a letter is cut off

parts.note: the conjunction losing its last letter
colic is severe abdominal pain

explanation.surface: Country life loses its charm when spoilt by agonising pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' looks like a mere conjunction in the surface, but it is the word that gets shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe rural life of shepherds and countryside, the subject of a genre of poetry.

clue.text: Mellow and unlikely to squeak

definitions.meaning: second meaning: lubricated, as a hinge treated with lubricant

explanation.walkthrough: The British slang sense, slightly drunk, is the one the first word points to; the second is literal lubrication.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses 'well oiled' for tipsy, and a lubricated hinge or wheel no longer creaks or squeals.

clue.text: Child slept and was taken for a book

parts.note: a kid is a child
had a nap

explanation.surface: A child dozed off and was mistaken for a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is defined twice: as a verb meaning abducted, and as Robert Louis Stevenson's novel about David Balfour.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone abducted has been seized and carried off; the Stevenson adventure novel bears this title.

clue.text: Henpecked bishop protruding, that is

parts.note: standing proud means sticking out from a surface
i.e., Latin id est

explanation.surface: A sticking-out bishop, browbeaten at home, is described.
explanation.walkthrough: Bishop Proudie in Trollope's Barchester novels is dominated by his formidable wife, Mrs Proudie.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's Barsetshire churchman is famously ruled by his domineering spouse, a literary character reference.

clue.text: Rise of record fever — died when harassed

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upward, the opposite direction

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing record
ague is a malarial fever
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A surge of record fever, and someone died while being pestered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' reads as a noun about soaring illness, but it tells you to read the record backwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To be pestered or tormented persistently is to be troubled, as if by a pestilence.

clue.text: Magic award — I'm satisfied

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire
a sigh of contentment

explanation.surface: Someone receives a wonderful honour and sighs contentedly.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE is an honour awarded by the British monarch, a common crossword award.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeah is a form of folk sorcery or witchcraft practised in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Dead men, so wrongly, got smothered

definitions.note: describes the person rather than naming her; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: something done wrongly is set out incorrectly, so the order is not to be trusted

parts.note: the fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Corpses were buried, wrongly, beneath something heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Othello the jealous Moor smothers his innocent wife with a pillow.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's wife dies by suffocation at her husband's hands, so she is the woman who met that fate.

clue.text: East German money under wraps, feature then of Berlin (6,6)

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
a facial feature as Berliners say it: Mund is German for mouth
the surname, not entered, comes from this part of the clue

explanation.surface: Communist cash kept secret was once a sight in the German capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Edmund Blunden, who wrote of the trenches; only his forename is entered. 'of Berlin' tells you the feature is in German.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble promises poets' names without definitions; Edmund Blunden was a First World War poet and later Oxford Professor of Poetry.

clue.text: Year in Paris was attractive proposition (6,6)

parts.note: an is French for year
drew in the sense of attracted
the surname, not entered: a proposition put to a meeting is a MOTION

explanation.surface: A year spent in the French capital was a tempting offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Andrew Motion, Poet Laureate from 1999; the forename is the one entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble promises poets' names without definitions; Andrew Motion was Britain's laureate when this puzzle appeared.

clue.text: Laodicean version of the North country

indicators.note: a version is a different rendering of the same material, here its letters

parts.note: the fodder, a word meaning lukewarm or half-hearted

explanation.surface: A lukewarm take on northern England or Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Laodicean, from the half-hearted church in Revelation, means indifferent; here it is only a set of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Caledonia is the old Latin name for Scotland, the land lying north of England.

clue.text: Salt source holding Derby

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Surrey town whose spring gave its name to a bath salt
second meaning: the town whose racecourse hosts the Derby each year

explanation.walkthrough: Derby looks like the Midlands city, but it is the famous flat horse race run on the Downs near this Surrey town.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom salts, magnesium sulphate, were first found in its mineral spring, and the racecourse there stages Britain's premier classic race.

clue.text: Where Croesus had all that bread — daily?

definitions.text: Where Croesus had all that bread

indicators.note: the question mark warns that the final word is not to be taken at face value but rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Asking whether the fabulously rich king got his loaves delivered every day.
explanation.walkthrough: Croesus was the immensely wealthy king of an ancient kingdom in Asia Minor; bread is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Croesus ruled this ancient kingdom of western Anatolia, proverbial for his enormous wealth.

clue.text: Unfinished or sent back with expression of disgust when upset

indicators.note: something sent back returns the way it came, so it reads in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and thrown into disorder

parts.note: the exclamation of revulsion
taken as written

explanation.surface: A half-done job is returned with a grimace by someone who is annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when upset' looks like the moment of annoyance, but the little word itself is the one to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber or stone cut into shape only crudely, without smoothing or polish, is left incomplete.

clue.text: Predatory tool

parts.note: surface reading: an instrument used for hunting prey
setter's reading: a person used as a dupe by another, named for a hunting animal's limb

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the fable of a monkey that uses a feline's foot to pull chestnuts from a fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe manipulated into doing someone's dirty work is an instrument, and the literal foot belongs to a hunting animal.

clue.text: Docile message about hot drink taking precedence

parts.note: a common drink

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: a cable is a telegram
H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A gentle note about a warm drink getting priority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking precedence' tells you the drink goes in front of the rest, though it comes last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A docile pupil is easily instructed and willing to learn, which is the sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Alfred and Frank (6,6)
She was at her ablutions, half naked, and David saw her

definitions.text: She was at her ablutions, half naked, and David saw her

indicators.note: only half of the word survives, the rest being cut away

parts.note: washing oneself
taken as written
the first half of BARE

explanation.surface: A woman bathing, partly undressed, is glimpsed by a king.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Old Testament King David sees her washing from his roof; the whole clue tells her story while the pieces build her name.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical wife of Uriah was spied bathing by King David, who then took her as his wife.

clue.text: Change barbarian country in the back row (6,6,6)

parts.note: ALTER, which with the W from the end of the row makes the forename WALTER, not entered
SAVAGE, the middle name, not entered
a land is a country

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: the word with its last letter cut off and passed to the forename

explanation.surface: Transform an uncivilised land sitting at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Walter Savage Landor; the clue builds all three names in turn, and the surname is the one entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble promises poets' names without definitions; Landor was a Romantic-era poet known for short lyrics and prose dialogues.

clue.text: Supporters' meeting at Twickenham or in the country?

parts.note: Twickenham is the home of English Rugby Union
a mass gathering of backers

explanation.surface: Fans gather either at the rugby stadium or out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Twickenham, in west London, is the national stadium of English Rugby Union, which is why it stands for the two-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something away from towns, among farms and fields, is doing it the rustic way.

clue.text: Don't talk to a girl with a weapon

parts.note: to cut someone is to snub them
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: Advice to ignore a young woman who is armed.
explanation.walkthrough: To cut someone dead is to ignore them pointedly, an old-fashioned social snub.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutlass is a short curved sword, the classic pirate's arm.

clue.text: Spooner's foolish friend (6,6)

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously mixed up the starts of words, so the opening sounds are exchanged

parts.note: silly is foolish and cobber is Australian slang for a mate; swapping the first sounds gives the poet's forename and surname

explanation.surface: A daft mate, as the muddle-mouthed Oxford don would put it.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Colley Cibber, an eighteenth-century actor and Poet Laureate mocked by Pope; the forename is the one entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble promises poets' names without definitions; Cibber held the laureateship and starred in Pope's satire The Dunciad.

clue.text: Food not cooked at home baffled the Crusaders

definitions.note: describes the man rather than naming him; the answer is a noun

parts.note: a dish of raw vegetables
at home means in

explanation.surface: Raw food eaten in the house puzzled the medieval knights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baffled the Crusaders' reads like the food's effect, but it describes the Muslim sultan who defeated them.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelfth-century sultan of Egypt and Syria recaptured Jerusalem and outmanoeuvred Richard the Lionheart's armies.

clue.text: Water and pulp for East African soldier (6,6)

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
MUSH without its H, which starts the surname
the rest of the surname, not entered: EA (East African) plus NEY, Napoleon's marshal

explanation.surface: Liquid and mush intended for a soldier from Kenya or Uganda.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Seamus Heaney, Nobel laureate: SEA plus MUS gives the forename, entered, and H, EA and NEY give HEANEY.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble promises poets' names without definitions; Heaney was the great Irish poet of Death of a Naturalist.

clue.text: Letter to painter in Hemp-stead, not to be preserved

indicators.note: a stead is a place taken by a substitute, so the letters stand in new positions

parts.note: HEMP, with the E that stands in for the A of Hampstead in this spelling

indicators.note: something put in another sits inside it, enclosed

parts.note: EL is the spelt-out name of the letter L
RA, Royal Academician, the usual crossword painter

explanation.surface: Writing to an artist who lives in a north London suburb, whose letters will be thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampstead is an artistic area of north London; the hyphenated misspelling flags HEMP and an E to rearrange. The painter goes inside the letter's name, and that follows the rearranged part.
explanation.definitionFit: Something short-lived and transient, like a leaflet or a mayfly, is not meant to last or be kept.

clue.text: Time London supplied fruit

indicators.note: the neighbouring words supply, or provide from their own stock, the letters needed

parts.note: the end of one word runs into the start of the next

explanation.surface: A period when the capital provided produce.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the gap between the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A large round fruit with sweet juicy flesh, such as a cantaloupe or watermelon.

clue.text: Home Counties friend in bloom

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a part found in a flower

parts.note: the Home Counties around London are in the South East
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A friend from the commuter belt is flowering.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties around London, all in England's South East. The definition is loose: a sepal is found in a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepals are the green leaf-like parts enclosing a flower bud, so one belongs to a blossom.

clue.text: Put down some wine

definitions.meaning: first meaning: set something down heavily

explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine; as a verb it means to drop something down carelessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are informal: dumping an object with a thud, and inexpensive table plonk bought by the bottle.

clue.text: Girl finding French gentleman an early victim

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for Monsieur
Abel, killed by Cain, the first murder victim in Genesis

explanation.surface: A young woman discovers a Frenchman who was among the first to be killed.
explanation.walkthrough: Abel, slain by his brother Cain in Genesis, is the Bible's first murder victim.
explanation.definitionFit: Mabel is a female given name, and crosswords treat any such name as a girl.

clue.text: Feudal superior, say, the back part being in cover

indicators.note: something that is in another sits inside it, enclosed

parts.note: a lid covers a container
e.g., for example

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: an actor's part

explanation.surface: A medieval overlord, for instance, with his hindquarters hidden under a blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the back part' looks like a body part; 'back' turns the part round and 'part' is an actor's role.
explanation.definitionFit: In the feudal system the vassal owed loyalty and service to the overlord above him.

clue.text: Pigs might fly? Barber seems (rudely) to imply it

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Flying Squad of the London police, rudely called pigs
second meaning: the murderous demon barber of Fleet Street in Victorian melodrama

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pigs might fly' looks like the saying for something impossible; it is rude slang for police in the Flying Squad, whose rhyming-slang name Sweeney Todd also belongs to the barber.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang calls the Flying Squad after the fictional Fleet Street barber, so police officers who fly share his name.

clue.text: First page embraced by Fanny (in the book) is in Gingerbread (6,6)

indicators.note: to be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, so one piece sits inside another
being in something means sitting inside it, so this whole group goes inside a further word

parts.note: I (first, as the Roman numeral one) plus P (page): these letters fall in the forename, so none are entered
HILL, from the novel Fanny Hill; only its final L reaches the entered name
PARKIN, a ginger cake from northern England; its P opens the forename

explanation.surface: The opening page of a racy novel turns up inside a gingerbread house.
explanation.walkthrough: IP sits inside HILL, giving HILIPL, and that sits inside PARKIN after its P: P-HILIPL-ARKIN spells PHILIP LARKIN, and only the surname is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble promises poets' names without definitions; Philip Larkin wrote The Whitsun Weddings and was a Hull librarian.
